title: Murphy’s Law
bubbles: If we don’t take umbrellas, it’ll rain.
sources: SB p.64–65 (PDF 65–66), Grammar Bank p.140–141 (PDF 141–142), Vocabulary Bank p.160 (PDF 161), Listening script 8.14 p.124 (PDF 125); WB p.56–57 (PDF 55–56), key WB p.92 (PDF 91). Scripts 8.13, 8.15–8.17 are not printed in the SB (answers by the recordings)

reference.title: First conditional
rows: If we get to the airport early,
If you tell her the truth,
if you don’t find a job?
If you miss the last bus,
If you miss the last bus,

reference.text: We use if + present to talk about a possible situation and will / won’t + infinitive to talk about the consequence.

reference.title: Word order
reference.text: The if-clause can come first or second. If the if-clause comes first, we usually put a comma before the next clause: If you don’t go, she won’t be pleased. / She won’t be pleased if you don’t go.

reference.title: Imperative or can
reference.text: We can also use the imperative or can + infinitive instead of will + infinitive in the other clause: If you miss the last bus, get a taxi. / If you miss the last bus, you can get a taxi.

reference.wrong: If it will rain, I’ll take an umbrella.
reference.right: If it rains, I’ll take an umbrella.
reference.why: After if we use the present, not will — even when we talk about the future.

reference.title: Confusing verbs
rows: a match, a medal, a prize
somebody for the first time, at 11 o’clock
that something good will happen, to do sth
for a bus, for a long time
your dictionary (to class), sth back from holiday
an umbrella (with you), your children to school
a joke, a lie, somebody something

reference.title: hope and expect
reference.text: hope = to want sth to happen, always for positive things, e.g. I hope I’ll pass the exam. expect = to think sth will happen, usually for a reason, e.g. I expect I’ll fail because I haven’t worked very hard.

reference.title: bring and take
reference.text: bring = movement towards here: Please bring your dictionaries to class tomorrow. take = movement away from here: Don’t forget to take all your things when you leave.

reference.wrong: The guide said Sue that there was only one tiger.
reference.right: The guide told Sue that there was only one tiger.
reference.why: tell somebody something; say something (to somebody) — say is never followed directly by a person.

tasks.instruction: Activation. Say a verb, your partner says a possible continuation. Then swap
tasks.note: VB Activation (A — глагол, B — продолжение) → разговор с ИИ

exercises.situation: Vocabulary game in an English class (level: pre-intermediate) with the confusing verbs: wear / carry, win / earn, know / meet, hope / wait, watch / look at, look / look like, miss / lose, bring / take, look for / find, say / tell, lend / borrow, hear / listen to. Take turns. First you say a verb (e.g. Wait…) and the student says a possible continuation (for a bus). If the continuation is wrong (e.g. earn a match, say me), say the correct pair briefly (No — win a match, earn money) and go on. After about six verbs, swap: the student says a verb and you give a continuation; sometimes make a small mistake on purpose (say a lie) and see if the student corrects you. Keep each turn very short.
exercises.goal: Say a good continuation for each verb, then give verbs to your partner.
exercises.opener: Let’s play! I say a verb, you finish it. Ready? Wait…
criteria: gives correct continuations for at least five verbs (wait for a bus, earn money, tell a lie…)
does not confuse the pairs (win / earn, say / tell, lend / borrow, hear / listen to)

reference.title: If something can go wrong…
reference.text: Murphy’s Law says: ‘If there is something that can go wrong, it will go wrong.’ It took its name from Captain Edward Murphy, an American aerospace engineer from the 1940s. Examples: if you change to a faster queue, your old queue will start moving faster; it will only rain if you forget your umbrella.

reference.title: Two Murphy’s Law stories
reference.text: Peter was unemployed for months. When a company finally phoned him about a job, he got cut off because his bus went into a tunnel. Sue chose the tiger trip on a free morning at a conference in Thailand — her group didn’t see the tiger, but the people on the bird trip did.

tasks.instruction: Read the first two paragraphs of the article and answer the questions
tasks.note: SB 1a (предсказание) + 1b «Who was Murphy? What is his ‘Law’?» → Blank по напечатанной статье
tasks.context: If something can go wrong… If you’re in a queue at the supermarket and you change to another queue which is moving more quickly, what will happen? The queue you were in before will suddenly start moving faster. What will happen if you take your umbrella because you think it’s going to rain later? It won’t rain, of course. It will only rain if you forget to take your umbrella. These are examples of Murphy’s Law, which says, ‘If there is something that can go wrong, it will go wrong’. Murphy’s Law took its name from Captain Edward Murphy, an American aerospace engineer from the 1940s. He was trying to improve safety for pilots flying military planes. Not surprisingly, he got a reputation for always thinking of the worst thing that could happen in every situation. Here are some more examples of Murphy’s Law.

tasks.instruction: Whose experience was more annoying? Have you ever had a Murphy’s Law experience?
tasks.note: SB 3d + SB 1d («Do any of these things often happen to you?») → разговор с ИИ

exercises.situation: Speaking practice in an English class (level: pre-intermediate) after the lesson ‘Murphy’s Law’ (‘If there is something that can go wrong, it will go wrong’). Two stories: Peter, unemployed for four months, finally got a call about a job on a bus, but was cut off in a tunnel and didn’t have the number (they called back the next day and he got the job). Sue chose the tiger trip at a conference in Thailand, didn’t see the tiger, but the people on the bird trip saw it. Laws from the article: if you order something online, you’ll be out when they deliver it; if you stop waiting for a bus and start walking, three will come at the same time; if you need to print a document urgently, the printer won’t have any paper; if you get to the airport early, your flight will be delayed. First ask the student whose experience was more annoying, Peter’s or Sue’s, and why; give your own opinion briefly. Then ask which of the laws often happen to them. Then ask about their own Murphy’s Law experience and ask two or three follow-up questions (When was it? What happened in the end?). Tell a short experience of your own too (e.g. you washed your car and it rained the same afternoon). Use the first conditional naturally (If I wash my car, it always rains!).
exercises.goal: Say whose experience was more annoying, and tell your own Murphy’s Law story.
exercises.opener: So, two stories — Peter and the phone call, Sue and the tiger. Whose experience do you think was more annoying?
criteria: says whose experience was more annoying and gives a reason
says which Murphy’s laws happen to them, using if + present, will + infinitive
tells a short personal story in the past simple

steps.example: I think Peter’s experience was more annoying, because he really needed the job.

steps.text: Which laws often happen to you?
steps.example: If I stop waiting for a bus and start walking, the bus always comes!

steps.text: Tell your own Murphy’s Law story
steps.example: Last year I got to the airport three hours early, and my flight was delayed.
